This is claim petition u/s 166/140 of M.V. Act seeking compensation in respect of death of late Gagan Sharma @ Gagan Jangra s/o Late Hawa Singh.

As per the facts mentioned in the claim petition, on 25.12.2021 at about 10.30 PM, the deceased was going on his motorcycle to Jangra Dharmshala, Dudhadhari Chowk, Bhupatal, Haridwar and when he reached at Pawan Dham Chowk,
Rashtriya Raj Marg, a vehicle bearing no. UK-07-TC-2633 (offending vehicle) came from behind at a very high speed, driven in a rash and negligent manner and hit the motorcycle of the deceased, as a result of which, the deceased fell down on the road and received grievous injuries.

It is further stated that injured was rushed to HMG District Hospital where he was declared brought dead and his postmortem was conducted in HMG Hospital, Haridwar vide Post Mortem No. 549/2021.
2.

I have gone through the record carefully and my issue wise findings are as under :
Issue No.1 9.
It is the settled proposition of law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v.
Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.

11. For the purpose of this issue, the testimony of PW-2 Sh. Manish Kumar, who is stated to be an eye witness of the accident in question, is very relevant.

He has deposed inter alia that on 25.12.2021 at about 10.30 PM, he was going in his car; that when he reached Pawan Dham Chowk, National Highway, Haridwar, he saw that a Bolero Car bearing no. UK07TC2633 hit a motorcyclist from behind; that he went near to the injured person, who was grievously injured with serious head injuries; that injured requested him to inform his family about the accident and he informed the wife of injured from his mobile phone about the accident.
He further deposed that the accident took place due to the rash and negligent driving on the part of driver of Bolero car no. UK-07-TC-2633.

PW2 deposed that he saw that a Bolero car/taxi hit the motorcyclist; that he was coming from Rishikesh to Haridwar.

He further deposed that the accident took place in front of his vehicle; that he noted down the number of offending vehicle and he was behind the place of accident around 15-20 feet.

He further deposed that the injured was in senses, who gave the telephone number of the residence and it was a mobile number; that he started his journey from his residence to Rishikesh in the morning on 25.12.2021.
He denied that he had not seen the accident or not present at the place of accident.
He denied of deposing falsely.
12. It is quite evident that the presence of PW-2 Sh. Manish Kumar at the spot is duly established.
PW-2 has categorically deposed about the mode and manner of the accident in question.
There is nothing material elicited from the cross examination of the aforesaid witness, which would impeach his credibility or trustworthiness.
PW-2 Sh. Manish Kumar, who is an independent witness, has given the full account of whatever took place in his presence at the spot at the time of accident.
He clearly stated in his cross examination that the accident took place in front of his vehicle and he noted down the number of the offending vehicle.
It is evident from the testimony of PW-2 that respondent could not impeach his testimony through litmus test of cross-examination.
Said witness is found to have successfully withstood the test of cross-examination.
There is no reason as to why he would depose falsely against the respondent no. 1 (driver of offending vehicle).
There is no possibility of false implication of respondent no. 1 and/or false involvement of offending vehicle by PW-2 at the instance of petitioners herein.

However, he did not enter into witness box during the course of inquiry.

Plea of the respondent no. 3 that it was deceased who was negligent due to which accident caused, has not been substantiated by any evidence.

The very factum that the offending vehicle had hit the motorcyclist from behind led to an inevitable conclusion that offending vehicle was being driven by the respondent no. 1 in a rash and negligent manner.

Issue No.2 19.
In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.

Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.

A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
Computation of Compensation 20.
The present case pertains to the death of deceased Sh. Gagan Sharma @ Gagan Jangra.

In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Said witness is found to have successfully withstood the test of cross-examination.
There is no reason as to why he would depose falsely against the respondent no. 1 (driver of offending vehicle).
There is no possibility of false implication of respondent no. 1 and/or false involvement of offending vehicle by PW-2 at the instance of petitioners herein.
Thus, FIR is shown to have been registered promptly and without any delay.
Hence, there is no possibility of false implication of respondent no. 1 and/or false involvement of aforesaid vehicle bearing No. UK-07-TC-2633 at the instance of petitioners herein.
16. Moreover, apart from petitioners, the respondent no. 1 Manish Kumar, driver of the offending vehicle, was the other material witness who could have thrown sufficient light as to how and under what circumstances, the accident in question took place.
However, he did not enter into witness box during the course of inquiry.
Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him for not entering into the witness box, to the effect that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle by him.
Plea of the respondent no. 3 that it was deceased who was negligent due to which accident caused, has not been substantiated by any evidence.
17. Moreover, in the given facts and circumstances of the present case, the rashness & negligence of the driver (R1) would also be assumed by virtue of res ipsa loquitur.
The very factum that the offending vehicle had hit the motorcyclist from behind led to an inevitable conclusion that offending vehicle was being driven by the respondent no. 1 in a rash and negligent manner.
In view of the finding on issue no.1, petitioners are entitled to get compensation, however, the quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.
Section 168 of Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) Ac 467 at page 492 per Lord Reid).
Computation of Compensation 20.
The present case pertains to the death of deceased Sh. Gagan Sharma @ Gagan Jangra.
In death cases, the guidelines for computation of compensation have been laid down by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121.
Petitioners have failed to bring any documentary proof or cogent evidence on record to show the vocation and income of the deceased.
Thus, for want of cogent and definite evidence being led by petitioners with regard to actual vocation and monthly income of deceased, this Tribunal assesses the income of the deceased to be at parity with minimum wages of Unskilled person in the State of Uttarakhand which at the time of accident was Rs. 9,211/- per month.
